lead: Momentum, heat and mass all cross the same thin fluid layer near a wall. In turbulent flow the same eddies carry all three. This shared motion lets one measured pressure drop predict a heat-transfer coefficient or a mass-transfer coefficient k_c. Engineers use it when a correlation is missing or when a quick check is needed, for example to estimate evaporation from a straight smooth duct using the skin-friction part of its pressure drop.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for k_c and Chapter 2.3 for Sh, Re and Sc, plus basic fluid mechanics (friction factor) and heat transfer (Nu, Pr).

blocks.text: In turbulent flow, a fluid packet carries momentum, enthalpy and solute together. Near a wall the total shear stress, heat flux and mass flux each have a molecular part and an eddy part. The eddy diffusivity for momentum, ε<sub>M</sub> (m²/s), for heat, ε<sub>H</sub>, and for mass, ε<sub>D</sub>, is nearly the same size when the turbulence is fully mixed. That shared eddy motion is the physical basis of every analogy here.

The three fluxes are τ = ρ(ν + ε<sub>M</sub>) du/dy, q/A = −ρ c<sub>p</sub>(α + ε<sub>H</sub>) dT/dy and N<sub>A</sub> = −(D<sub>AB</sub> + ε<sub>D</sub>) dC<sub>A</sub>/dy. Here τ is shear stress (Pa), q/A is heat flux (W/m²), N<sub>A</sub> is molar flux (mol/(m²·s)), ν is kinematic viscosity (m²/s), α is thermal diffusivity (m²/s), D<sub>AB</sub> is molecular diffusivity (m²/s), and y is distance from the wall (m).

Two dimensionless groups compare molecular transport: Pr = ν/α = μ c<sub>p</sub>/k and Sc = ν/D<sub>AB</sub> = μ/(ρD<sub>AB</sub>). Pr is the Prandtl number (dimensionless), Sc the Schmidt number, μ viscosity (Pa·s), c<sub>p</sub> specific heat (J/(kg·K)), k thermal conductivity (W/(m·K)).

blocks.where: St = h/(ρ c<sub>p</sub> u) is the Stanton number; h is the heat-transfer coefficient (W/(m²·K)); u is bulk velocity (m/s); f is the Fanning friction factor, defined by τ<sub>w</sub> = f (1/2) ρ u², with τ<sub>w</sub> the wall shear stress (Pa).

blocks.text: This is the Reynolds analogy. It says the dimensionless temperature profile and the dimensionless velocity profile have the same shape when Pr = 1. It is quick but narrow: it ignores the laminar sublayer.

Chilton and Colburn kept the same idea but absorbed the molecular-property effect into j-factors. The heat j-factor is j<sub>H</sub> = Nu/(Re Pr<sup>1/3</sup>). The mass j-factor is j<sub>D</sub> = Sh/(Re Sc<sup>1/3</sup>). Here Nu = hL/k<sub>f</sub> is the Nusselt number, Sh = k<sub>c</sub>L/D<sub>AB</sub> is the Sherwood number, and Re = ρuL/μ is the Reynolds number; L is the characteristic length (m), k<sub>f</sub> is fluid thermal conductivity (W/(m·K)), and k<sub>c</sub> is the mass-transfer coefficient (m/s). For a flat plate, L is the plate length. For pipe flow, the characteristic length is the pipe diameter D, so use Re = ρuD/μ, Sh = k<sub>c</sub>D/D<sub>AB</sub>, and Nu = hD/k<sub>f</sub>.
j<sub>H</sub> = Nu/(Re Pr<sup>1/3</sup>) = f/2,   j<sub>D</sub> = Sh/(Re Sc<sup>1/3</sup>) = f/2
blocks.where: j<sub>H</sub> and j<sub>D</sub> are dimensionless; f is the Fanning friction factor; all other symbols are defined above. Hence j<sub>H</sub> = j<sub>D</sub> = f/2.

blocks.text: The equality is used to estimate k<sub>c</sub> from a measured pressure drop. Follow these steps.

items: Measure Δp (Pa) over a smooth pipe length L (m) at bulk velocity u (m/s) and density ρ (kg/m³); D is the pipe diameter (m) and L is the length between pressure taps.
Get the Fanning friction factor from Δp = 2f(L/D)ρu², so f = Δp D/(2Lρu²).
Compute Sc = μ/(ρD<sub>AB</sub>) and Re = ρuD/μ. Use D, not L, as the characteristic length for pipe flow.

blocks.text: For a flat plate, use the local or average skin-friction coefficient from boundary-layer tables in place of the pipe formula. The j-factor route is the same. For a flat plate use L as the characteristic length in Nu = hL/k<sub>f</sub>, Sh = k<sub>c</sub>L/D<sub>AB</sub>, and Re = ρuL/μ. The analogy is popular in compact heat exchangers and drying because pressure drop is easy to measure, while k<sub>c</sub> is not.

Prandtl-Taylor and von Kármán refined the analogy by keeping the laminar sublayer. Prandtl-Taylor gives St = (f/2)/[1 + 5√(f/2)(Pr − 1)] for heat transfer, and the same form with Sc for mass transfer. von Kármán adds the buffer layer and gives a better fit when Pr or Sc is far from 1, such as oil (Pr about 1000) or a liquid with Sc in the thousands, such as salts or sugars in water. Gases have Sc about 0.6, close to 1, and the simple analogy handles them well.

The analogy assumes skin friction, not form drag. A pressure drop across a valve, a bend or a rough packing includes form drag, so the f you calculate is too large. The predicted k<sub>c</sub> is then too high. It also assumes small mass-transfer rates. Strong blowing or suction changes the velocity profile and breaks j<sub>D</sub> = f/2; use a high-mass-transfer correction or a direct correlation in that case.

figure.caption: Momentum, heat and mass join through the same eddy diffusivity; the Chilton-Colburn result sets j_H = j_D = f/2, here 0.004.

spec.title: Chilton-Colburn analogy

examples.question: Air flows over a smooth flat plate. The Fanning friction factor is f = 0.008. Estimate j<sub>D</sub>, Sh and k<sub>c</sub> for Re = 5×10⁴, Sc = 0.6, D<sub>AB</sub> = 2.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s and L = 0.5 m.
examples.check:
import math
f = 0.008
Re = 5e4
Sc = 0.6
D_AB = 2.5e-5
L = 0.5
j_D = f / 2
Sc13 = Sc ** (1/3)
Sh = j_D * Re * Sc13
k_c = Sh * D_AB / L
print(round(j_D, 3))
print(round(Sc13, 3))
print(round(Sh, 1))
print(round(k_c, 4))

traps: Using the Darcy friction factor instead of the Fanning factor. Darcy f is four times Fanning f; j<sub>D</sub> = f/2 needs Fanning. A factor-of-four error gives k<sub>c</sub> four times too large.
Taking f from a pressure drop that includes form drag. The analogy uses wall skin friction only. Valves, bends and rough packings give a high f and a high predicted k<sub>c</sub>.
Applying j<sub>D</sub> = j<sub>H</sub> = f/2 at high mass-transfer rates. Blowing or suction alters the boundary layer. Use a correction or a direct correlation.

Mixing the exponents: j<sub>D</sub> uses Sc<sup>1/3</sup> in the denominator; the mass Stanton number follows j<sub>D</sub> = St<sub>m</sub> Sc<sup>2/3</sup>. Write the definition before substituting.
Forgetting units: Sh and Re are dimensionless; D<sub>AB</sub> is m²/s; L is m; k<sub>c</sub> comes out in m/s.

quiz.q: Define the Fanning friction factor f and the Stanton number St. State the Reynolds analogy for Pr = 1.
quiz.a: τ<sub>w</sub> = f (1/2)ρu², so f = 2τ<sub>w</sub>/(ρu²). St = h/(ρc<sub>p</sub>u). Reynolds analogy: St = f/2 when Pr = 1.

quiz.q: Why does equality of eddy diffusivities let a friction factor predict k<sub>c</sub>?
quiz.a: The same turbulent eddies carry momentum and solute, so the dimensionless velocity and concentration profiles have the same shape. Wall shear and mass flux then scale together, giving j<sub>D</sub> = f/2.

quiz.q: For f = 0.01, Re = 2×10⁴ and Sc = 2.0, find j<sub>D</sub> and Sh.
A student measures pressure drop across a 90° elbow and uses it to predict k<sub>c</sub> on a flat plate. Will k<sub>c</sub> be too high or too low? Explain.
quiz.a: Too high. The elbow pressure drop is mostly form drag, so the calculated f is larger than the skin-friction value. j<sub>D</sub> = f/2 then overpredicts Sh and k<sub>c</sub>.

quiz.q: Write j<sub>H</sub> and j<sub>D</sub> in terms of Nu, Sh, Re, Pr and Sc.
quiz.a: j<sub>H</sub> = Nu/(Re Pr<sup>1/3</sup>); j<sub>D</sub> = Sh/(Re Sc<sup>1/3</sup>).

quiz.q: What do Prandtl-Taylor and von Kármán add to the Reynolds analogy?
quiz.a: They keep the laminar sublayer (Prandtl-Taylor) and also the buffer layer (von Kármán). This improves predictions when Pr or Sc is far from 1.

quiz.q: If j<sub>H</sub> = 0.006 and Pr = 1, estimate f and St.
quiz.a: j<sub>H</sub> = f/2, so f = 0.012. For Pr = 1, St = j<sub>H</sub> = 0.006.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern CFD uses the same eddy-diffusivity idea in k–ε and k–ω turbulence models, but solves local transport instead of one j-factor. Compact heat-exchanger design still uses Colburn j-factors because they combine heat transfer and pressure drop in one plot. High-mass-flux corrections appear in ablation cooling and in drying of wet solids. Search for Chilton-Colburn analogy, Reynolds analogy and high mass transfer rate correction.
